title: Def recommend sitting close for this one #thesharkisbroken #broadway
transcript: I was invited to go see The Shark Is Broken on Broadway. And a couple disclaimers. Again, I was invited. I did not pay for this ticket. And I also saw this first preview. Before our first preview, this show was in really good shape, and I thoroughly enjoyed myself. The Shark Is Broken is a play that takes place behind the scenes during the filming of jaws. It centers around the 3 main actors as they are on the boat filming all of the boat scenes. Notoriously, during the filming of jaws, the shark would break all of the time. So they had all of this downtime on this boat in the middle of the ocean. And so this play takes place during all of the hypothetical conversations that these performers were having with each other as they were waiting for the shark to be fixed. And that is the play. There's not really a narrative structure to this. It is a series of these conversations. And I think that people expecting that narrative structure are going to be disappointed by the show. But I thoroughly enjoyed myself because these conversations were so freaking compelling. So many of them have to deal with legacy and what we end up leaving behind on multiple levels. When you have the level of the fact that this play is co written and stars Ian Shaw playing his own father, Robert Shaw, and at times it almost felt like I was watching one Of Ian Shaw therapy sessions, but, like, in the best way possible. There's a lot of conversations about father and sons and what we end up leaving to children. There's also this idea of legacy in terms of, like, the fact that all of these actors are filming what is literally the film that invented the summer blockbuster, but they don't actually realize that in the moment. Also where a lot of the comedy in this show comes from. The scenes themselves aren't funny, but the circumstances and what we know as an audience are what makes it funny at times. And there's also this layer of talking about legacy in terms of artists, where you have Richard Dreyfus, who's at the beginning of his career, having conversations with Robert Shaw, who is literally at the end of his career, and the dynamic that that creates between the 2 of them. Ultimately, I found this show really, really compelling, but it's definitely not going to be for everyone. If you are looking for a narrative structure, if you are looking for situational comedy, it's less that and more of just existential ideas on what we end up leaving behind and how art impacts other people. And the performances are absolutely stellar. Obviously, you have Ian Shah, who is amazing playing his own father. You also have Colin Donnell and Alex Brightman, both of who I have been a fan of for forever in musical theater. And so it was really Really great to see them really be able to dig into this really compelling play. And yes, Alex Brightman really is that good in this show. I could see him potentially getting a nomination depending on how the plays shape up the season. It's very early. My one complaint about this show is I wish some of the transitions were directed just a little smoother. But I do feel like that is something that can be smoothed out during the preview period, and so I hope it does cause that. That was. That was my one caveat, but ultimately, I really enjoyed this. I saw it for free, but you can get $30 in person rush tickets and their front row, which is the perfect seat for the
